data.content_ref: inline:The claim's mechanism justifies the selection rule — 'Select the hypothesis that has withstood the most stringent attempts at refutation' — by appealing to forward-looking benefits: the hypothesis 'contains more empirical content and thus offers more opportunities for future learning if it is false.' This is an expectation of future utility. Yet the claim's own first countercondition stipulates that 'if one insists that "preference" implies an expectation of future success, then Popper's position collapses into hidden induction.' The mechanism's justification — that past-surviving theories will 'offer more opportunities for future learning' — is precisely such an expectation. The claim thus triggers its own refutation condition: it denies making future-oriented claims while simultaneously grounding its rule in them. The non-inductive logical property invoked (empirical content) cannot do the justificatory work alone, because it is a present-tense property of a theory independent of whether the theory has survived tests. The selection rule discriminates on the basis of past survival (an inductive input), not content alone (a non-inductive property). If two theories have identical empirical content but different test-survival records, the rule selects the survivor, but the content-based justification applies to both equally — exposing that the operative criterion is past performance projected forward, i.e., hidden induction.
